newsitem.title: UK: SUGAR-Russia buys Brazil cargoes, shipments smooth.
newsitem.headline: SUGAR-Russia buys Brazil cargoes, shipments smooth.

text.p: Sugar shipments from Brazil's centre-south growing area are proceeding with fewer logistical problems than last year with Russia heading the list of destinations, brokers said on Friday.
Cargoes traded on a cost and freight basis (C&F) were dominating the market, while quotes for free on board (FOB) sugars were thin on the ground, they said.
"We're seeing very little FOB business at all...there's not much there, certainly not on a prompt basis," said one physical trader. "Most of the trading is being done cost and freight."
Market sources quoted C&F raws cargoes at premiums of around $35/45 over October futures, likely to be trading at $37 over, for spot arrival into the Black Sea.

According to the latest monthly report from Czarnikow Sugar, the insistence of Russian buyers on taking prompt raws partially reflected their lack of available financing. Russian refineries were also starting to close down in advance of the domestic beet crop, it noted.
Apart from occasional cargoes moving across to both west and east Africa, demand for Brazilian sugars -- both raws and whites -- was most prevalent from Russia's Black Sea and Baltic ports.

"The Russians are still buying but they're only interested in a spot/spot basis," said another trader, who also mentioned smaller amounts finding their way into Georgia and the former Soviet states in central Asia.
Market sources cited talk that at least 30,000 tonnes of Brazilian whites had recently been imported into the Russian Baltic, and possibly significantly more.
Logistically, brokers said one of the greatest problems over the last month had been heavy rains in south Brazil -- in addition to the run of strikes and go-slows usual for this time of the year.
The centre-south is now seeing warm and dry weather virtually throughout the region which has brought cane crushings of the 1997/98 harvest back to normal, particularly since the start of July.
Improved loading at Santos, the highest volume port in South America which handles the largest variety of cargo in Brazil, has also helped matters.
Traders said ships were arriving, loading and departing at Santos much more quickly than last year, with the turnaround in some cases reported to be as quick as two to three days.
"It's certainly been a vast improvement on last year," the first physical trader said.
Sugar shipments out of key centre-south ports reached 441,825 tonnes in June, around 50 percent higher than the 294,981 tonnes shipped in June last year.
